lessons.title: Ozymandias — Power & Its Decay
lessons.description: How Shelley uses irony and imagery to show that even the mightiest rulers are ultimately powerless.
lessons.content_html:
Percy Bysshe Shelley and Romantic Rebellion

Ozymandias was written by Percy Bysshe Shelley in 1817, during a period of intense political upheaval across Europe. Shelley was a radical who opposed monarchy and tyranny. He believed that power structures were temporary and that nature would always outlast human ambition. The poem was written in a friendly competition with fellow poet Horace Smith, and both poets chose the same subject — the fallen statue of Ramesses II.

Key Fact

Ozymandias is the Greek name for the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II, who ruled for 66 years (c. 1279–1213 BC) and was one of the most powerful rulers in ancient history. Shelley uses his ruined statue to show that all power eventually crumbles.

The Poem’s Structure and Framing

Shelley uses a framing narrative — the speaker tells us what “a traveller from an antique land” said. This creates layers of distance: we hear from a speaker, who heard from a traveller, about a sculptor who depicted a king. Each layer removes us further from Ozymandias’s actual power, reinforcing how completely it has faded.

The poem is a sonnet, but Shelley deliberately breaks the conventional rhyme scheme (ABAB ACDC EDE FEF instead of the regular Petrarchan or Shakespearean pattern). This irregularity mirrors the destruction of Ozymandias’s empire — the traditional form of the sonnet is “ruined” just as the statue is.

“Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert” — The statue is fragmented and incomplete. The adjective “trunkless” emphasises that the body (and therefore the power it represented) has been destroyed. The verb “Stand” is ironic: the legs still stand, but the ruler they represented has fallen.

“Half sunk, a shattered visage lies” — The plosive alliteration in “half” and the sibilance in “sunk” and “shattered” create a sense of violent destruction. The face is buried in sand, symbolising how time erases even the most powerful figures.

“sneer of cold command” — The sculptor captured Ozymandias’s cruelty and arrogance in stone. The alliterative “c” sounds are harsh, reflecting the king’s ruthless authority. Ironically, the sculptor’s art has outlasted the king’s power — art endures where tyranny does not.

“Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” — This is the inscription on the pedestal, spoken in Ozymandias’s own voice. The imperative “Look” and the exclamation mark show his arrogance and desire to intimidate. The dramatic irony is devastating: the “Works” have vanished entirely, so the boast now reads as a warning about the futility of pride.

Themes

Power of nature over human power: The desert has swallowed everything Ozymandias built. The “lone and level sands stretch far away” — the vast, empty landscape dominates the final image. Nature is presented as the ultimate power, indifferent to human achievement.

Transience of political power: Ozymandias commanded an empire, yet nothing remains. Shelley, writing during a time of revolution, suggests that all tyrants will eventually fall. The poem can be read as a direct challenge to rulers of Shelley’s own era.

Key Fact

The final image — “The lone and level sands stretch far away” — uses alliteration of the soft “l” sound and a long, sweeping rhythm to convey the vastness of the desert and the total erasure of Ozymandias’s empire.

An often-overlooked theme is the power of art. The sculptor “well those passions read / Which yet survive” — the artist understood Ozymandias’s character so well that the emotions carved in stone still communicate centuries later. The sculptor’s skill outlasts the king’s power. For Shelley, a poet, this is a powerful statement: creative expression endures where political power does not.

The phrase “the hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed” contains a double meaning. “Mocked” can mean both “imitated” (the sculptor copying the expressions) and “ridiculed” (the sculptor subtly mocking the king through art). This ambiguity enriches the poem’s exploration of power.

Comparison Opportunities

With My Last Duchess: Both poems explore how powerful men try to control others, but while the Duke’s power over the Duchess persists through the painting, Ozymandias’s power has been entirely eroded. Both involve art as a record of character.

With London: Both poets criticise abuse of power — Shelley through the ancient tyrant, Blake through the institutions of Georgian London. Both suggest that oppressive power structures are ultimately destructive.

With The Prelude: Both present nature as more powerful than humanity. In The Prelude, the mountain terrifies the speaker; in Ozymandias, the desert has consumed an empire.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the comparison question, don’t just describe what happens in each poem — compare how the poets present their ideas. For Ozymandias, focus on Shelley’s use of irony and the broken sonnet form. A strong response will analyse the effect of specific language choices (e.g. “sneer of cold command”) and link them to Shelley’s radical political beliefs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shelley uses the ruined statue of Ozymandias to argue that all political power is temporary — nature and time will always win.
  • The broken sonnet form mirrors the destruction of the statue and the empire it represents.
  • Key techniques to analyse include dramatic irony, the framing narrative, alliteration, and the contrast between the boastful inscription and the empty desert.

lessons.title: London & Checking Out Me History
lessons.description: How Blake and Agard challenge power structures and give voice to the oppressed.
lessons.content_html:
William Blake’s ‘London’

William Blake wrote ‘London’ in 1794 as part of his collection Songs of Experience. The poem is a scathing attack on the institutions Blake saw as responsible for human suffering: the Church, the monarchy, and the government. Blake walked through the streets of London and what he saw — poverty, child labour, prostitution — shaped this angry, despairing poem.

Key Fact

Blake wrote during the early Industrial Revolution, when rapid urbanisation had created terrible living conditions for the poor. The poem was also written five years after the French Revolution (1789), which Blake initially supported as a symbol of people overthrowing oppressive power.

“I wander thro’ each charter’d street, / Near where the charter’d Thames does flow” — The repetition of charter’d is deeply ironic. A charter is meant to grant freedoms, but Blake uses the word to suggest everything is owned, controlled, and restricted. Even the Thames — a natural river — has been claimed by those in power.

“Marks of weakness, marks of woe” — The repetition of “marks” suggests both physical signs of suffering and the metaphorical “marks” branded onto people by an oppressive system. The noun “woe” is absolute and inescapable.

“mind-forg’d manacles” — This powerful metaphor suggests that people are mentally imprisoned. The “manacles” are not physical chains but psychological ones — the people have been conditioned to accept their oppression. The compound adjective “mind-forg’d” implies the chains are both created by and locked within the mind.

“every black’ning Church appalls” — “Black’ning” refers literally to soot from factories staining church walls, but also metaphorically to the moral corruption of the Church. The verb “appalls” carries a double meaning: to shock, and to cast a “pall” (a funeral cloth) over the institution. Blake accuses the Church of being complicit in suffering.

“the hapless Soldier’s sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls” — The synaesthesia of a sigh turning into blood on walls creates a horrifying image. The “Palace” (capitalised to represent the monarchy) is stained by the blood of soldiers sent to die in wars. Blake blames the ruling class directly.

“the youthful Harlot’s curse / Blasts the new-born Infant’s tear” — The final stanza is the most disturbing. The young prostitute’s suffering (a “curse” — both swearing and disease) destroys even the innocence of a newborn. The verb “Blasts” is violent and explosive. Blake shows that poverty corrupts everything, even the next generation.

Structure and Form of ‘London’

The poem has four quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme, creating a steady, relentless rhythm like the speaker’s footsteps through the streets. The anaphora of “In every” in stanza two hammers home the universality of suffering — no one is exempt. The poem moves from observation (stanza 1) to analysis (stanzas 2-3) to a devastating conclusion (stanza 4), building in intensity.

John Agard’s ‘Checking Out Me History’

John Agard wrote this poem to protest the Eurocentric education system he experienced. The poem alternates between mocking the “history” he was taught in British schools (Guy Fawkes, Dick Whittington, Lord Nelson) and celebrating the Black and Caribbean historical figures who were deliberately excluded from the curriculum.

Key Fact

Agard uses Caribbean Creole dialect (“Dem tell me”) throughout the poem. This is a deliberate political choice — it asserts his Caribbean identity in a poem about cultural erasure and challenges the dominance of Standard English in education and literature.

“Dem tell me / Dem tell me / Wha dem want to tell me” — The angry refrain uses repetition to emphasise how controlled the education was. “Dem” represents the white British establishment. The Caribbean dialect is itself an act of resistance against the language imposed by colonisers.

“Toussaint / a slave / with a vision / lick back / Napoleon / battalion” — The short, punchy lines about Toussaint Louverture create a powerful, rhythmic energy. The verb “lick back” (Caribbean dialect for “fought back”) is forceful and physical. The contrast between “a slave” and defeating “Napoleon / battalion” highlights the extraordinary achievement.

“a healing star / among the wounded / a yellow sunrise / to the dying” — Mary Seacole is described using natural imagery: “star,” “sunrise.” This elevates her to something almost divine, contrasting with the mundane British figures (Dick Whittington and his cat). The metaphors suggest she brought hope and life to the hopeless.

“But now I checking out me own history / I carving out me identity” — The shift to the present tense shows the speaker taking control. “Carving” suggests active, physical effort — reclaiming identity is hard work, not passive. The rhyme of “history” and “identity” links the two concepts: understanding your history is essential to knowing who you are.

Comparison: Blake and Agard

Both poets use their poems as acts of political protest. Blake attacks the Church, monarchy, and government for causing suffering in Georgian London; Agard attacks the education system for erasing Black history and identity. Both use repetition as a structural device (Blake’s “In every”; Agard’s “Dem tell me”) to build a sense of relentless injustice. However, while Blake’s tone is despairing and the poem ends with no hope, Agard’s poem ends with empowerment: “I carving out me identity.”

Both poets challenge who holds power over narratives. Blake shows how institutions control people’s lives; Agard shows how institutions control people’s understanding of history. Both suggest that true freedom requires breaking free from these controls.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing these poems with others in the anthology, focus on the poets’ methods rather than just their messages. Compare how Blake uses a strict ABAB rhyme scheme to create a relentless mood, while Agard uses irregular line lengths and dialect to rebel against conventional poetic form. Always link form and structure to meaning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Blake’s ‘London’ is a furious attack on institutional oppression, using “mind-forg’d manacles” to suggest people are psychologically as well as physically trapped.
  • Agard’s ‘Checking Out Me History’ protests the erasure of Black history in British education, using Caribbean dialect and contrasting structures to assert cultural identity.
  • Both poems challenge power structures, but Blake’s ends in despair while Agard’s ends with empowerment and reclamation.

lessons.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade & Bayonet Charge
lessons.description: How Tennyson and Hughes present the reality of battle through rhythm, imagery, and contrasting attitudes to war.
lessons.content_html:
Tennyson’s ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’

Alfred, Lord Tennyson wrote this poem in 1854, shortly after reading a newspaper report about the disastrous cavalry charge at the Battle of Balaclava during the Crimean War. Due to a miscommunication in orders, 600 British soldiers on horseback charged directly into Russian cannons. Around 110 were killed, 160 wounded, and 375 horses destroyed. Tennyson wrote the poem in minutes, driven by admiration for the soldiers’ obedience and courage.

Key Fact

As Poet Laureate, Tennyson had an official role to write for the nation. His poem commemorates the bravery of ordinary soldiers while subtly criticising the commanders whose “blunder” caused the disaster. The poem was published in The Examiner newspaper and was widely read by the Victorian public.

“Half a league, half a league, / Half a league onward” — The poem opens with driving dactylic rhythm that mimics the galloping of horses. The repetition creates a sense of unstoppable momentum — the soldiers cannot turn back. A league is approximately three miles; the repetition emphasises the vast distance they must cover under fire.

“Into the valley of Death” — An allusion to Psalm 23 (“the valley of the shadow of death”). The capitalisation of “Death” personifies it as a force waiting for them. The valley is also literal — the soldiers rode into a valley surrounded by cannon on three sides.

“Some one had blunder’d” — Tennyson acknowledges the catastrophic military error, but does not name the person responsible. The vague “Some one” deflects blame from any individual, keeping the focus on the soldiers’ bravery rather than the leaders’ incompetence.

“Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die” — The triple repetition of “Theirs” emphasises the soldiers’ unquestioning obedience. The rhyme of “why” and “die” links questioning with death — obedience is their only option. This can be read as both admiration for their duty and a quiet criticism of a system that demands blind obedience.

“Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them” — The repetition surrounds the reader just as the cannons surround the soldiers. The three directions create a claustrophobic trap. “Volley’d and thunder’d” uses onomatopoeia to bring the sounds of battle to life.

“Honour the charge they made! / Honour the Light Brigade” — The imperative “Honour” is a direct instruction to the reader. Tennyson commands us to remember and respect these men, turning the poem into a memorial.

Ted Hughes’s ‘Bayonet Charge’

Ted Hughes wrote ‘Bayonet Charge’ from the imagined perspective of a World War I soldier mid-attack. Unlike Tennyson, Hughes does not celebrate or commemorate — he exposes the terror, confusion, and absurdity of combat. Hughes’s father survived the Gallipoli campaign, and this personal connection shapes the poem’s raw intensity.

Key Fact

Hughes begins the poem in medias res (in the middle of the action) with the word “Suddenly.” There is no buildup, no context, no patriotic framing — the reader is thrown into the chaos just as the soldier is, reflecting the disorientation of combat.

“Suddenly he awoke and was running” — The abrupt opening disorients the reader. “Awoke” suggests the soldier has been in a trance-like state; the violence has shocked him into consciousness. The present continuous “was running” creates immediacy.

“raw-seamed hot khaki, his sweat heavy” — The compound adjectives and tactile imagery make the reader feel the soldier’s physical discomfort. “Raw-seamed” suggests the uniform is chafing his skin, reducing the heroic soldier to a suffering body.

“King, honour, human dignity, etcetera / Dropped like luxuries” — The dismissive “etcetera” is devastating. The abstract concepts that supposedly justify war (King, honour, dignity) are treated as meaningless afterthoughts. “Dropped like luxuries” suggests they are discarded under the pressure of survival — in the moment of combat, ideology is worthless.

“a yellow hare that rolled like a flame” — The simile compares the injured hare to a flame, linking nature with the violence of war. The hare’s suffering mirrors the soldier’s — both are innocent victims caught in destruction they don’t understand. The image is both beautiful and horrifying.

Comparing the Two Poems

Attitude to war: Tennyson commemorates and honours the soldiers; Hughes strips away all heroism and glory. Tennyson’s repetitive, galloping rhythm creates energy and momentum; Hughes’s irregular, fractured lines mirror the soldier’s confusion. Tennyson’s soldiers are a collective (“the six hundred”); Hughes focuses on a single, anonymous individual.

Use of form: Tennyson uses regular stanzas and a driving rhythm; Hughes uses three stanzas of unequal length with enjambment that creates a breathless, stumbling pace. Both poets use sound devices, but for opposite effects: Tennyson’s onomatopoeia (“thunder’d”) creates dramatic spectacle, while Hughes’s harsh consonants (“raw-seamed hot khaki”) create physical discomfort.

Context: Tennyson wrote as Poet Laureate with a patriotic duty; Hughes wrote from a twentieth-century perspective shaped by two world wars and a more critical attitude towards military authority.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing these poems, the strongest responses will examine how the poets’ different contexts shape their attitudes. Tennyson, writing as Poet Laureate in 1854, had a duty to honour the soldiers; Hughes, writing after two world wars, could afford to be more critical. Always embed context within your analysis of language and structure — don’t treat it as a separate paragraph.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tennyson uses galloping dactylic rhythm, repetition, and imperatives to commemorate the Light Brigade’s bravery while subtly acknowledging the “blunder” that caused the disaster.
  • Hughes uses in medias res, fractured enjambment, and the dismissive “etcetera” to strip away all heroism and expose the raw terror of combat.

lessons.title: My Last Duchess — Power & Control
lessons.description: How Browning uses the dramatic monologue to reveal the Duke’s obsessive need for control and ownership.
lessons.content_html:
Robert Browning and the Dramatic Monologue

Robert Browning published ‘My Last Duchess’ in 1842. The poem is a dramatic monologue — the Duke of Ferrara speaks to an envoy who has come to negotiate his next marriage. As the Duke describes a painting of his “last Duchess,” he inadvertently reveals that he had her killed because she was too friendly, too easily pleased, and refused to submit entirely to his control.

Key Fact

The poem is based on Alfonso II, Duke of Ferrara, whose first wife, Lucrezia de’ Medici, died in suspicious circumstances in 1561 at the age of 17. Alfonso then negotiated to marry the niece of the Count of Tyrol. Browning uses this historical basis to explore themes of male power, objectification, and possessiveness.

The Duke’s Character

The Duke is possessive, controlling, and deeply proud. He sees people as objects to be owned. He controls access to the painting — “since none puts by / The curtain I have drawn for you, but I” — just as he controlled (and ultimately destroyed) the Duchess herself. The curtain is a physical symbol of his power: only he decides who sees her, even in death.

His pride in his “nine-hundred-years-old name” reveals his obsession with social status. The Duchess’s crime, in his eyes, was treating his aristocratic name as equal to other pleasures — a sunset, a cherry branch, a mule ride. She did not value his status above all else, and for this, she was destroyed.

“That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall, / Looking as if she were alive” — The possessive “my” immediately establishes ownership. “Last” is chilling — it implies there will be another. “Looking as if she were alive” is simultaneously a compliment to the painter and a sinister reminder that she is now dead.

“She had / A heart — how shall I say? — too soon made glad” — The caesura created by “how shall I say?” mimics the Duke choosing his words carefully, performing politeness while expressing a deeply sinister criticism. The Duchess’s “crime” was being joyful and kind to everyone — she was “too soon made glad.”

“I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together” — This is the poem’s most chilling moment. The euphemism is deliberate — “gave commands” hides the reality of murder behind bureaucratic language. “All smiles stopped” is a devastating understatement. The semicolon creates a pause that mirrors the finality of death.

“Notice Neptune, though, / Taming a sea-horse” — The final image is a bronze sculpture of Neptune (god of the sea) taming a sea-horse. This is a metaphor for the Duke: he sees himself as a god, taming those beneath him. The Duchess was his “sea-horse” — something wild and beautiful that he needed to control.

Form and Structure

The poem is written in rhyming couplets with iambic pentameter, but the enjambment frequently disguises the rhymes, making the poem sound like natural speech. This reflects the Duke’s character: beneath his polished, conversational surface lies rigid control. The rhyming couplets represent his obsessive need for order, while the enjambment shows his attempts to seem casual and reasonable.

The poem is a single, unbroken stanza — the Duke monopolises the conversation, never allowing the envoy (or the reader) to interject. His control of the narrative mirrors his desire to control everything around him. The silent listener is powerless, just as the Duchess was.

Key Fact

Browning’s use of the dramatic monologue means the Duke condemns himself with his own words. He thinks he is presenting himself as reasonable and justified, but the reader sees a controlling, murderous tyrant. This gap between the Duke’s self-perception and the reader’s perception is the poem’s central irony.

With Ozymandias: Both poems feature powerful men whose pride defines them. However, Ozymandias’s power has crumbled into nothing, while the Duke’s power appears intact — he is about to acquire another wife. Both poems explore how art preserves character: the sculptor captured Ozymandias’s “sneer”; Fra Pandolf captured the Duchess’s blush.

With Poppies: Both poems explore relationships, but from opposite perspectives. The Duke treats the Duchess as a possession; the mother in ‘Poppies’ expresses genuine love and grief. The Duke controls through silencing (“all smiles stopped”); the mother is silenced by loss.

With London: Both explore the abuse of power, but in different forms. Blake criticises institutional power (Church, monarchy); Browning exposes personal, domestic tyranny. Both poets suggest that power corrupts.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The dramatic monologue is the most important technique to analyse in this poem. Explain how the Duke reveals more than he intends — he thinks he’s justified, but the reader sees a murderer. This gap between what the speaker says and what the reader understands is called dramatic irony, and discussing it will earn you marks for analysis of the writer’s methods (AO2).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Browning uses the dramatic monologue form to let the Duke condemn himself — he inadvertently reveals his possessiveness, pride, and the murder of his wife.
  • Key quotations to learn: “I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together,” “That’s my last Duchess,” and the Neptune/sea-horse metaphor.
  • The rhyming couplets represent control, the enjambment mimics natural speech, and the single stanza shows the Duke’s monopoly over the conversation.

lessons.title: Exposure & Storm on the Island
lessons.description: How Owen and Heaney present nature as a powerful, destructive force that overwhelms and threatens humanity.
lessons.content_html:
Wilfred Owen’s ‘Exposure’

Wilfred Owen wrote ‘Exposure’ while serving in the trenches during the winter of 1917–18. The poem describes the agonising experience of soldiers waiting in freezing conditions, slowly dying not from enemy fire but from the cold itself. Owen’s purpose is to show that the greatest enemy in war is not the opposing army but nature — and the government that sent the soldiers there.

Key Fact

Owen was diagnosed with shell shock (now called PTSD) and sent to Craiglockhart Hospital in Edinburgh, where he met Siegfried Sassoon. Owen returned to the front and was killed on 4 November 1918, exactly one week before the war ended. His mother received the telegram on Armistice Day.

“Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knive us” — The opening line personifies the wind as a killer (“knive us”). The verb is brutally direct. The sibilance in “merciless iced east” mimics the hissing of wind. The ellipsis that follows (“wearied we keep awake...”) creates a sense of exhausted waiting.

“But nothing happens” — This refrain ends four of the eight stanzas. Its repetition creates a devastating sense of futility. The soldiers are not dying heroically in battle — they are dying from cold, boredom, and neglect. Each repetition drains more hope from the poem.

“Pale flakes with fingering stealth come feeling for our faces” — The alliteration of “f” sounds personifies the snow as something sinisterly gentle, like fingers searching for skin. The snow is both beautiful and deadly — it “feels” for them, as if death itself is reaching out.

“The burying-party, picks and shovels in their shaking grasp, / Pause over half-known faces” — The final stanza describes the burial of the dead. “Half-known faces” is devastating — the cold has so disfigured the bodies that their comrades can barely recognise them. The present tense makes this immediate and ongoing.

Structure of ‘Exposure’

Owen uses eight stanzas of five lines each, with a shortened final line in each stanza (called a half-line). This “dying fall” mirrors the soldiers slowly losing strength and life. The para-rhyme (e.g. “wire/war,” “snow/renew”) creates an unsettling sense of incompleteness — nothing quite resolves, just as the soldiers’ situation never resolves.

Seamus Heaney’s ‘Storm on the Island’

Seamus Heaney published ‘Storm on the Island’ in 1966. On the surface, the poem describes a community on a remote island bracing for a violent storm. However, the title contains a hidden message: “Stormont” (the seat of the Northern Irish government) is embedded in “Storm on the Island,” suggesting the poem is also about the political turmoil of The Troubles.

Key Fact

The first eight letters of the title spell “STORMONT” — the Northern Irish parliament building. Heaney, a Catholic growing up in Protestant-dominated Northern Ireland, often embedded political messages within seemingly natural imagery.

“We are prepared: we build our houses squat” — The confident, declarative opening suggests readiness and resilience. “We” establishes a collective community identity. “Squat” means low and sturdy — built to withstand attack. If read politically, this suggests a community preparing for conflict.

“the wizened earth has never troubled us / With hay” — The enjambment creates a momentary surprise. The earth hasn’t “troubled” them with growing hay — i.e. nothing grows here, so there’s nothing for the wind to destroy. The barren landscape is presented as an unexpected advantage.

“spits like a tame cat / Turned savage” — The simile compares the sea to a domesticated animal that suddenly becomes wild. The familiar becomes frightening. If read politically, this mirrors how communities can turn violent during conflict.

“It is a huge nothing that we fear” — The paradoxical ending is deeply unsettling. The storm is invisible — wind has no physical form — yet it terrifies them. This suggests that the greatest fears are intangible: the threat of violence, political uncertainty, the unknown. The oxymoron “huge nothing” captures the paradox of fearing something you cannot see or control.

Comparing Owen and Heaney

Both poets present nature as a hostile, overwhelming force. Owen’s soldiers are killed by cold: “nothing happens” — the enemy is absence, exposure, waiting. Heaney’s community fears a “huge nothing” — the storm is terrifying precisely because it is invisible and unpredictable. Both poems end without resolution: Owen’s soldiers are buried; Heaney’s community is left in fear.

Structurally, Owen uses para-rhyme and half-lines to create discord and incompleteness; Heaney uses blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) and enjambment to create a conversational, almost reassuring tone that is gradually undermined. Both poets use the “we” pronoun to create collective experience — this is not individual suffering but shared, communal vulnerability.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Both poems explore the power of nature, but the strongest exam responses will distinguish between their purposes. Owen uses nature to criticise war and the government that sends soldiers to die; Heaney uses nature as a metaphor for political fear during The Troubles. Always specify which poem you are analysing and avoid generalising about “both poets.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Owen’s ‘Exposure’ presents the cold as a more deadly enemy than the opposing army, using para-rhyme and the refrain “But nothing happens” to convey futility and despair.
  • Heaney’s ‘Storm on the Island’ uses a literal storm as a metaphor for political fear, with the title hiding “Stormont” and the ending revealing that the community fears a “huge nothing.”
  • Both poems present nature as an overwhelming, uncontrollable force and use the collective “we” to show shared vulnerability.

lessons.title: Remains & War Photographer
lessons.description: How Armitage and Duffy present the lasting psychological impact of conflict on those who witness it.
lessons.content_html:
Simon Armitage’s ‘Remains’

Simon Armitage based ‘Remains’ on the real testimony of a soldier called Guardsman Tromans, who served in Iraq. The poem appeared in the 2008 documentary film The Not Dead, which explored PTSD in returning soldiers. The speaker describes shooting a looter in Basra and then being haunted by the memory of the killing, unable to wash the blood from his mind.

Key Fact

The poem is a dramatic monologue based on real testimony. Armitage uses colloquial, conversational language (“probably armed, possibly not”) to reflect how soldiers actually speak, making the psychological trauma feel authentic and immediate rather than literary or distant.

“probably armed, possibly not” — This devastating admission comes early. The soldier doesn’t know whether the man he killed was a threat. The modal verbs “probably” and “possibly” create uncertainty — and it is this uncertainty that torments him. The casual, almost throwaway delivery makes it more disturbing: this moral ambiguity is presented as routine.

“One of my mates goes by / and tosses his guts back into his body” — The brutal, graphic imagery strips away any dignity from death. The casual verb “tosses” is shocking — a human body is treated like rubbish. This reflects the dehumanising effect of war on both the dead and the living.

“His blood-shadow stays on the street” — The compound noun “blood-shadow” and the image of the dead man “wandering” suggests the victim haunts the speaker. The dead man has followed the soldier home — he cannot escape what he has done, even in England.

“his bloody life in my bloody hands” — The repetition of “bloody” works as both literal description (blood on his hands) and colloquial swearing (expressing frustration). This double meaning captures the soldier’s guilt and anger simultaneously. He is responsible for a death he can never undo.

“I blink / and he bursts again through the doors of the bank” — The present tense “bursts” shows the memory replaying in real time. Every time the speaker blinks, the killing happens again. This is a powerful depiction of PTSD — the traumatic memory is involuntary, intrusive, and inescapable.

Structure of ‘Remains’

The poem begins with regular four-line stanzas, reflecting the soldier’s attempt to tell the story in an ordered, controlled way. But the final stanza breaks into just two lines: “his bloody life in my bloody hands.” The form literally breaks down as the soldier’s mental control collapses. The shift from past tense (the event) to present tense (the flashbacks) marks the poem’s turning point — the killing is over, but the trauma is ongoing.

Carol Ann Duffy’s ‘War Photographer’

Carol Ann Duffy wrote ‘War Photographer’ based on the experiences of real conflict photographers, particularly Don McCullin. The poem explores the moral tension between documenting suffering and the public’s indifference to it. The photographer develops his images in a darkroom in rural England, surrounded by peace, while the photographs reveal the horrors of war.

Key Fact

Duffy structures the poem around the contrast between “Rural England” (peaceful, indifferent) and the war zones the photographer has visited: “Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.” The three-word list uses short, blunt proper nouns to represent real suffering, while England is associated with comfortable ignorance.

“In his darkroom he is finally alone / with spools of suffering set out in ordered rows” — The sibilance in “spools of suffering” creates a quiet, mournful tone. The metaphor of “ordered rows” echoes both film negatives and rows of graves — the photographs are records of death. “Finally alone” suggests he needs solitude to process what he has witnessed.

“a priest preparing to intone a Mass” — The simile compares the photographer’s work to a religious ritual. Developing photographs becomes a sacred act — a ceremony of remembrance for the dead. This elevates photography from journalism to something reverential and solemn.

“a half-formed ghost” — As the photograph develops in the chemical solution, the dead man’s face appears like a ghost. The image is both literal (the photograph developing) and metaphorical (the dead man haunting the photographer). This links to ‘Remains’ — both speakers are haunted by the dead.

“The reader’s eyeballs prick / with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers” — The final stanza is bitterly ironic. The newspaper readers feel a momentary pang of emotion, but it is sandwiched between trivial domestic comforts. “Prick” suggests the emotion is tiny and superficial. Duffy criticises the public for their shallow response to real suffering.

Comparing Armitage and Duffy

Both poems explore the psychological aftermath of conflict, but from different perspectives. Armitage’s soldier is directly involved in the violence and cannot escape his guilt; Duffy’s photographer is a witness who feels the moral burden of documenting suffering that the public ignores. Both speakers are trapped: the soldier by flashbacks, the photographer by a cycle of documenting horror that changes nothing.

Structurally, Armitage uses colloquial language and broken form to mirror psychological breakdown; Duffy uses controlled stanzas and religious imagery to convey quiet, dignified grief. Both poems end without resolution — the trauma continues.
lessons.exam_tip_html: These poems are frequently compared in the exam. To reach the top levels, analyse how both poets use form to convey psychological states: Armitage’s collapsing stanza structure reflects PTSD; Duffy’s controlled quatrains reflect the photographer’s attempt to impose order on chaos. Always link your analysis of language and structure to the poets’ purposes.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Armitage’s ‘Remains’ uses colloquial language, graphic imagery, and a collapsing stanza structure to depict PTSD with raw authenticity.
  • Duffy’s ‘War Photographer’ uses religious imagery and bitter irony to criticise public indifference to the suffering documented by conflict photographers.
  • Both poems show that the psychological impact of conflict extends far beyond the battlefield — it follows people home and never fully resolves.

lessons.title: Kamikaze & The Emigrée
lessons.description: How Garland and Rumens explore the conflict between personal identity and the power of place, memory, and society.
lessons.content_html:
Beatrice Garland’s ‘Kamikaze’

Beatrice Garland wrote ‘Kamikaze’ from the perspective of a daughter telling the story of her father, a Japanese kamikaze pilot who turned his plane around instead of completing his mission. The poem explores the devastating consequences of this decision: his family and community treat him as though he no longer exists, shaming him into a living death.

Key Fact

In Japanese culture during WWII, kamikaze pilots were considered heroes making the ultimate sacrifice for the Emperor. To refuse a mission was the deepest possible dishonour. The pilot’s family would have been shamed by his return, and the community would have treated him as dead — a fate many considered worse than actual death.

“Her father embarked at sunrise / with a flask of water, a samurai sword” — The opening is deceptively calm. “Sunrise” suggests a new beginning, not an ending. The “samurai sword” connects the pilot to the ancient warrior code of bushido, which demanded death before dishonour.

“a shaven-headed full moon” — The metaphor compares the grandfather’s shaved head to the moon. This is a moment of tender, personal memory in a poem about national ideology. The grandfather represents the human life that the pilot is being asked to throw away.

“the dark shoals of fishes / flashing silver as their bellies / swivelled towards the sun” — The vivid natural imagery represents life, beauty, and freedom — everything the pilot would lose. The fish turning “towards the sun” mirrors his own turn away from death. Nature reminds him of what it means to be alive.

“they treated him / as though he no longer existed” — After his return, the pilot is socially dead. His family “no longer spoke to him.” This silence is a form of psychological punishment more cruel than physical death — he chose life, but was given a living death instead.

“he must have wondered / which had been the better way to die” — The devastating final line reveals that both options led to death: physical death in the mission, or social death at home. The poem questions whether his choice to live was worth it.

Structure of ‘Kamikaze’

The poem uses indirect speech (“my mother / she said that”) rather than letting the pilot speak directly. He is silenced even within the poem, just as he was silenced by his community. The shift from third person narrative to the daughter’s first person reflection at the end marks the poem’s emotional turn.

Carol Rumens’s ‘The Emigrée’

Carol Rumens wrote ‘The Emigrée’ from the perspective of someone who left their homeland as a child and clings to idealised memories of it, even though the country has since been consumed by conflict. The speaker’s memory is “sunlight-clear” — bright, warm, and unblemished — despite the reality of war and oppression.

Key Fact

The title uses the feminine French form “Emigrée” (with the accent), indicating the speaker is female. An emigrée is someone who has left their country, often for political reasons. Rumens deliberately leaves the country unnamed — the poem could apply to any exile from any conflict.

“There once was a country... I left it as a child” — The fairy-tale opening (“There once was”) immediately establishes nostalgia and loss. The country exists only in memory, like a story. “As a child” explains why the memories are idealised: a child’s perspective filters out complexity.

“my memory of it is sunlight-clear” — The compound adjective “sunlight-clear” dominates the poem. Light imagery recurs constantly, making the memories glow with warmth and beauty. This brightness resists every negative update about the country.

“They accuse me of being dark in their free city” — The pronoun “They” is ominous and vague — representing society, perhaps racists, perhaps the government. “Dark” could refer to skin colour, foreignness, or the suspicion directed at immigrants. The irony of “free city” is sharp: the city claims freedom but persecutes the outsider.

“My city takes me dancing through the city / of walls” — The personified city from her memory “dances” with her, suggesting joy and freedom. This contrasts with the “city of walls” — her current reality of barriers, exclusion, and hostility. The internal rhyme and flowing rhythm capture the grace of the memory.

Comparing Garland and Rumens

Both poems explore the conflict between individual identity and the power of society or place. The kamikaze pilot is destroyed by social rejection; the emigrée is sustained by personal memory despite social hostility. Both speakers are defined by an impossible choice: the pilot chose life over duty and was punished; the emigrée clings to a homeland that no longer exists as she remembers it.

Both poems use light imagery: in ‘Kamikaze’, the fish “swivelled towards the sun” — beauty that calls the pilot back to life. In ‘The Emigrée’, the memory is “sunlight-clear” — light that defies reality. Both suggest that personal experience and memory can be more powerful than politics or ideology.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Both poems work well for comparison questions about identity, memory, or the impact of conflict on individuals. When analysing ‘Kamikaze’, focus on the structural silencing of the pilot (indirect speech, no direct quotation). For ‘The Emigrée’, focus on the recurring light imagery and how it resists every negative update. Always connect techniques to meaning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • ‘Kamikaze’ shows how social pressure and cultural duty can be more destructive than war itself — the pilot chose life but received a living death through family silence and rejection.
  • ‘The Emigrée’ presents memory as a form of resistance — the speaker’s idealised, sun-drenched memories of her homeland cannot be corrupted by war, politics, or prejudice.
  • Both poems explore how individuals are shaped by forces beyond their control — cultural expectations, exile, conflict — and the choices they make in response.

lessons.title: Tissue & Poppies
lessons.description: How Dharker and Weir use everyday objects as symbols to explore power, fragility, and the human cost of conflict.
lessons.content_html:
Imtiaz Dharker’s ‘Tissue’

Imtiaz Dharker uses paper as an extended metaphor for the fragility of human-made structures — buildings, borders, money, maps, and even identity. The poem argues that everything humans build is ultimately as thin and temporary as tissue paper. Dharker suggests this fragility should be embraced, not feared: if we built the world from paper, it would be “turned into your skin” — human and vulnerable rather than rigid and oppressive.

Key Fact

Dharker references the “Koran” (Qur’an) as “the kind of paper / thinned by age or touching.” This links the sacred text to the poem’s central argument: even holy scripture is physical, fragile paper that wears thin over time. Nothing humans create — not even religion — is permanent.

“Paper that lets the light / shine through” — The recurring image of light passing through paper suggests transparency and openness. Dharker argues that if structures (governments, borders) were transparent like paper, they would be more human and less oppressive. Light also symbolises truth and understanding — paper that “lets the light shine through” reveals rather than conceals.

“Maps too. The borderlines, the marks / that rivers make, roads, / railtracks, mountainfolds” — The listing technique collapses natural features (rivers, mountains) together with human constructs (roads, railtracks, borderlines). Dharker suggests that borders are as artificial as the paper they are drawn on — nature does not recognise human boundaries.

“turned into your skin” — The final twist reveals that the ultimate “tissue” is human skin. This shifts the poem from abstract philosophy to something deeply personal. Skin is the most fragile structure of all — and the most important. Dharker suggests that human vulnerability is more valuable than any building, border, or institution.

“might fly our lives like paper kites” — The simile imagines lives as paper kites: light, free, and joyful, but also fragile and at the mercy of the wind. This celebrates impermanence rather than fearing it. The image is playful and optimistic, contrasting with the poem’s earlier references to borders and money.

Structure of ‘Tissue’

The poem uses short, four-line stanzas that are themselves “thin” like tissue paper. The enjambment between stanzas creates a flowing, continuous movement — ideas spill across boundaries, just as the poem argues that human constructs should be more fluid. The final stanza is a single, isolated line (“turned into your skin”), standing alone on the page like a revelation. The form enacts the poem’s content: it is delicate, layered, and ultimately personal.

Jane Weir’s ‘Poppies’

Jane Weir wrote ‘Poppies’ from the perspective of a mother whose son has gone to war. The poem is set on Armistice Day and moves between the domestic (pinning a poppy to his blazer) and the battlefield (hoping to hear his voice “on the wind”). Weir was commissioned to write the poem for a 2009 anthology exploring the effects of conflict, and she chose to focus on the private grief of a parent rather than the public spectacle of war.

Key Fact

The poem does not specify which war or whether the son is alive or dead. This ambiguity is deliberate — the poem represents the universal experience of a parent losing a child to conflict. The domestic details (smoothing a blazer, making the cat hairs disappear) ground the poem in the everyday, making the grief more tangible.

“I pinned one onto your lapel, crimped petals, / spasms of paper red, disrupting a blockade / of yellow bias binding around your blazer” — The poppy becomes a symbol linking remembrance (red), violence (“spasms”), and disruption. The noun “spasms” is visceral — even the symbol of remembrance carries violence within it.

“Sellotape bandaged around my hand” — The domestic object (Sellotape) is compared to a bandage, linking household activities with the wounds of war. This textile imagery runs throughout the poem, connecting the mother’s domestic world with her son’s experience of conflict.

“On reaching the top of the hill I traced / the inscriptions on the war memorial, / leaned against it like a wishbone” — The mother traces the memorial as a surrogate act of touching her son. “Wishbone” reveals her fragile hope. The physical gesture of leaning makes the scene intensely personal and intimate.

“I listened, hoping to hear / your playground voice catching on the wind” — The final image is devastating. The mother goes to the war memorial and listens for her son’s childhood voice. “Playground voice” juxtaposes innocence with the reality of war. The separation between past (childhood) and present (conflict/death) is unbridgeable.

Comparing Dharker and Weir

Both poems use the fragility of paper/tissue as a central motif. Dharker uses it abstractly — paper represents all human constructs. Weir uses it concretely — the “tissue paper” of the poppy represents both remembrance and the fragility of human life. Both poems ultimately argue that human vulnerability is at the heart of everything: Dharker’s poem ends with “skin,” Weir’s with a mother’s love.

Structurally, Dharker uses short, thin stanzas that mirror paper; Weir uses longer, flowing stanzas that mirror the continuous stream of a mother’s memory. Both poets use enjambment to create flowing, uncontainable emotion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about ‘Tissue’, many students struggle because the poem is abstract. Focus on the extended metaphor of paper and explain what each type of paper represents (Qur’an = faith, maps = borders, receipts = money, skin = humanity). For ‘Poppies’, focus on the textile/domestic imagery and how it connects the mother’s world to the battlefield. Both poems reward close attention to individual words and images.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • ‘Tissue’ uses paper as an extended metaphor for the fragility of all human constructs — borders, money, buildings — and argues that human skin is the most important “tissue” of all.
  • ‘Poppies’ presents a mother’s private grief as more powerful than any public narrative about war, using domestic and textile imagery to connect the home with the battlefield.
  • Both poems celebrate human vulnerability and suggest that fragility — of paper, poppies, skin, and love — is what makes us most fully human.

lessons.title: The Prelude — Power of Nature
lessons.description: How Wordsworth uses the stolen boat episode to show nature humbling human confidence and revealing a greater power.
lessons.content_html:
William Wordsworth and Romanticism

William Wordsworth wrote The Prelude between 1798 and 1850. It is a vast autobiographical poem about the growth of the poet’s mind, and the extract studied for AQA comes from Book 1, in which the young Wordsworth steals a boat and rows across a lake at night. What begins as a confident, joyful adventure becomes a terrifying encounter with the power of nature, as a mountain appears to rise up and pursue him.

Key Fact

Wordsworth was a leading figure of the Romantic movement, which valued emotion over reason, nature over industry, and the individual over society. The Romantics believed nature had a spiritual, almost divine power that could transform human consciousness. This extract dramatises that belief through the boy’s terrifying encounter with the mountain.

The Stolen Boat Episode

The extract divides into three clear stages. First, the boy discovers a boat and rows out onto the lake in a state of youthful confidence and pleasure. Second, a mountain appears to rise up and chase him, shattering his confidence. Third, the boy returns the boat and is haunted for days by “huge and mighty forms” in his imagination. This three-part structure mirrors a moment of revelation — the boy’s understanding of his place in the world is permanently altered.

“One summer evening (led by her) / I found a little Boat tied to a Willow tree” — Nature (“her”) is personified as a guiding female figure, leading the boy to the boat. The calm, pastoral language (“summer evening,” “Willow tree”) establishes an idyllic mood. The boy feels in harmony with nature.

“lustily / I dipped my oars into the silent lake” — The adverb “lustily” conveys youthful energy and confidence. The “silent lake” is calm and unthreatening. The boy is enjoying himself, unaware of what is about to happen. The verb “dipped” is gentle — he disturbs the water only lightly.

“a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary purpose, it upreared / Its head” — The mountain is personified as a living creature that rises up with “voluntary purpose” — it seems to choose to terrify the boy. The repetition of “huge” and the harsh consonants in “black” and “peak” create a sense of overwhelming, menacing scale. The mountain “Strode after me” — it pursues him like a predator.

“with trembling oars I turned, / And through the silent water stole my way / Back to the covert of the Willow tree” — The boy’s confidence has collapsed. “Trembling” replaces “lustily.” He “stole” back — a word linking back to his original theft of the boat, but now suggesting fear and guilt rather than adventure. The “Willow tree” reappears, but the return journey feels entirely different from the departure.

“huge and mighty forms, that do not live / Like living men, moved slowly through the mind” — The aftermath is psychological. The “forms” are not real — they exist in his mind — but they are described as more real than “living men.” Nature has planted something in his consciousness that will never leave. The slow rhythm of “moved slowly through the mind” suggests these images are permanent and inescapable.

Themes

The sublime: The mountain represents the Romantic concept of the sublime — something so vast and powerful that it inspires both awe and terror. The boy is humbled: he thought he was in control of nature (rowing the boat), but nature showed him he is insignificant. This encounter changes him permanently.

Nature’s moral authority: The boy stole the boat — a transgression. Nature’s response (the mountain rising) can be read as a punishment or warning. Wordsworth presents nature as having a moral dimension: it teaches, corrects, and humbles humanity. The boy returns the boat “with grave / And serious mood,” suggesting he has learned a lesson.

Key Fact

The shift from confidence to fear is reflected in the poem’s language: “lustily” becomes “trembling,” “proud” becomes “grave,” and the “silent lake” becomes a space of terror. This reversal is the poem’s central movement — from human confidence to natural dominance.

With Ozymandias: Both poems show nature overwhelming human power. In Ozymandias, the desert has erased an empire; in The Prelude, the mountain terrifies a boy. Both suggest that nature is the ultimate power, indifferent to human ambition.

With Exposure: Both present nature as hostile and overwhelming. Owen’s soldiers are killed by the cold; Wordsworth’s boy is psychologically transformed by the mountain. However, Wordsworth sees this as ultimately positive (a learning experience), while Owen sees only destruction.

With Storm on the Island: Both explore humanity’s vulnerability to nature. Heaney’s community faces a “huge nothing”; Wordsworth faces a “huge peak, black and huge.” Both poets use the word “huge” to convey nature’s overwhelming scale.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The extract from The Prelude is one of the best poems for comparison questions about the power of nature, conflict between humanity and nature, or the concept of the sublime. When analysing it, track the shift in language from confidence to fear (e.g. “lustily” to “trembling”). This demonstrates understanding of structure and the writer’s methods, which examiners specifically reward.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Wordsworth presents nature as a vast, living force that humbles human confidence through the concept of the sublime — the mountain terrifies the boy and permanently changes his understanding of his place in the world.
  • The poem’s three-part structure (confidence → terror → haunted aftermath) mirrors the boy’s psychological transformation.
  • Key techniques include personification of nature, the contrast between “lustily” and “trembling,” and the haunting final image of “huge and mighty forms” moving through the mind.

lessons.title: Comparing Poems & Exam Skills
lessons.description: How to structure a top-level comparison response, with planning strategies and model paragraph techniques.
lessons.content_html:
The Comparison Task

Your anthology comparison will give you one named poem from the cluster and ask you to compare it with another poem of your choice on a shared theme. The task rewards candidates who can hold two texts in mind at once and draw precise, insightful links between them. Plan your time so you finish with a few minutes spare for checking — planning, writing and proofreading are all part of a strong response. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact wording and timing.

Key Fact

Strong comparative essays balance three skills in every paragraph: a personal, argued response anchored in precise quotations; close analysis of the poets’ methods (language, structure, form); and contextual understanding woven in rather than bolted on. Accurate written expression also matters — slips in spelling and grammar make analysis harder to follow.

Choosing Your Second Poem

Your choice of second poem is crucial. Choose a poem that allows you to make meaningful comparisons, not just surface-level connections. The best choices will share a theme but present it differently — through contrasting attitudes, forms, or contexts. For example, if given ‘Remains’ (guilt and PTSD), comparing with ‘War Photographer’ (witnessing trauma) allows you to compare two different relationships with conflict.

Power of nature: The Prelude + Exposure, Storm on the Island + Ozymandias

Effects of conflict: Remains + War Photographer, Bayonet Charge + Exposure, Poppies + Kamikaze

Power and control: My Last Duchess + Ozymandias, London + Checking Out Me History

Identity and place: The Emigrée + Kamikaze, Checking Out Me History + The Emigrée

Memory and loss: Poppies + Remains, The Prelude + Kamikaze, War Photographer + The Emigrée

Attitudes to war: Charge of the Light Brigade + Bayonet Charge, Exposure + Remains

Planning Your Response

Spend a few minutes planning before you write. Use the 3-point plan: identify three points of comparison, each with a quotation from both poems and a note on the method used. A strong plan might look like this:

Key Fact

Example plan (theme: effects of conflict):
1. How conflict is experienced — “probably armed, possibly not” (Remains, moral ambiguity) vs “spools of suffering” (War Photographer, witnessing)
2. Psychological aftermath — “his bloody life in my bloody hands” (Remains, guilt/PTSD) vs “half-formed ghost” (WP, haunting)
3. Form and structure — collapsing stanzas (Remains, breakdown) vs controlled quatrains (WP, imposed order)

Writing a Comparative Paragraph

Each paragraph should follow the PEALC structure: Point (a comparative statement), Evidence (quotation from poem A), Analysis (method and effect), Link (quotation from poem B with comparison), Context (relevant background). Crucially, you must compare throughout the paragraph, not write about one poem and then the other.

Model: Both poets present speakers who are haunted by the violence they have witnessed, though they respond to it differently. In ‘Remains’, Armitage uses the present tense — “he bursts again through the doors of the bank” — to show the killing replaying involuntarily, a hallmark of PTSD that reflects the psychological toll on soldiers returning from Iraq. Similarly, Duffy’s photographer sees a “half-formed ghost” as the image develops — a metaphor that works both literally (the developing photograph) and figuratively (the dead man haunting him). However, while Armitage’s soldier is consumed by guilt (“his bloody life in my bloody hands”), Duffy’s photographer is consumed by the futility of documenting suffering that the public ignores: “eyeballs prick with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers.” This bitter irony reflects Duffy’s anger at a society that treats real human suffering as a momentary inconvenience.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Writing about one poem then the other: This is the most common mistake. You must compare within each paragraph, using connectives like “similarly,” “in contrast,” “whereas,” and “however.” Essays that treat the poems in separate halves rarely reach the top bands, however strong the individual analysis.

Feature-spotting without analysis: Naming a technique (e.g. “Shelley uses alliteration”) is not enough. You must explain the effect of that technique and link it to the poet’s purpose. Ask: Why did the poet choose this word/technique? What does it make the reader feel or think?

Bolting on context: Context should be woven into your analysis, not added as a separate sentence. Instead of “Blake wrote during the Industrial Revolution,” write: “Blake’s use of ‘charter’d’ reflects the commodification of public space during the Industrial Revolution, when even the Thames was controlled by commercial interests.”

For similarities: Similarly, Likewise, In the same way, Both poets, This is echoed in, [Poet B] also

For differences: In contrast, Whereas, However, Conversely, Unlike [Poet A], While [Poet A]… [Poet B]

For nuanced comparison: Although both poets… they differ in, While the theme is shared, the methods contrast, Where [Poet A] uses… [Poet B] instead employs
lessons.exam_tip_html: Aim for three comparative paragraphs in 45 minutes (5 minutes planning, 35 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking). Each paragraph should discuss both poems together. The strongest responses will compare not just what the poems say (AO1) but how they say it (AO2 — language, structure, form) and why (AO3 — context). Remember: you choose the second poem, so pick one you know well and can analyse in detail.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The comparison question requires you to compare two poems throughout your response — never write about one poem and then the other.
  • Choose your second poem carefully: the best comparisons involve poems that share a theme but present it differently through contrasting methods and contexts.
  • Use the PEALC structure (Point, Evidence, Analysis, Link, Context) to ensure every paragraph addresses all three Assessment Objectives.
